newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA WHEAT CROP GETS MORE RAIN BUT NEEDS MORE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA WHEAT CROP GETS MORE RAIN BUT NEEDS MORE.

text.p: More steady rain overnight in Australia's southern and eastern grain belt had stabilised the crop for the time being, the Australian Wheat Board's (AWB) crop forecaster Michael Shean said on Friday.
But unless additional rain was received from South Australia through to Queensland, there was further downside potential for the crop, he said.
"This hasn't saved us. You're not likely to see the crop estimate rise," he said.
Current 1997/98 crop estimates range from 14 million to 15.3 million tonnes, down from the record 23.6 million last season.
Either more rain of the type just received was required every second week, or much heavier rain was required less frequently than that, Shean said.
The El Nino weather pattern would still be a major factor over the rest of the growing season, which for wheat lasts through until about March, and was not disappearing, he said.
Sea surface temperatures were continuing to warm. Hopefully the drought effect would end by next planting season, he said.
Good overnight falls of five mm to 15 mm occurred in southwest and lower western crop areas in the state of New South Wales (NSW), a Bureau of Meteorology official told Reuters.
The state of Victoria had similar falls.
In the 48 hours to Friday morning, falls in Victorian wheat-growing areas were about the 20 mm mark, ranging from nine to almost 30 mm, a state weather official said.

In South Australia, overnight falls ranged from about 14 mm in the state's upper north to about five mm on the Eyre Peninsula. Most other areas had falls of about five to 10 mm although the lower south region recorded a highest fall of 21 mm, a South Australian weather official said.
The outlook is for more scattered rain, weather officials said.
